pages.title: The Three Pillars of Radiation Protection

content.text: Radiation protection is the protection of people from the harmful effects of ionizing radiation exposure. It's achieved through three principles:

Dose limits are set by the NCRP and follow a

Notice the general public limit is consistently 1/10 of the occupational limit for the same site — a pattern worth remembering rather than memorizing each number in isolation.

Is a pregnant worker required to disclose her pregnancy to become a Declared Pregnant Worker?
NCRP guidance treats disclosure as voluntary — the DPW status and its added protections only begin once she chooses to notify her supervisor.

The radiation protection "watchdog" — makes dose limit recommendations
Provides international recommendations and guidance; no enforcement authority

Every institution using radiation-producing equipment or radioactive materials must have a
, who specifies required survey meters and dosimeters, supervises their calibration and proper use, and reviews personnel dose reports for anomalies.
Beyond personal dosimeters, several instruments detect and measure radiation in the environment or at the treatment unit:
Counts ion pairs; calibrates linear accelerators and measures treatment beam characteristics
Gas-filled tube, audible signal; surveys rooms/personnel after implants, finds lost sealed sources
Surveys high-radioactivity storage areas and around machines like HDR units
Sodium iodide crystal + photomultiplier tube; highly sensitive, mainly used in nuclear medicine
Gas-filled neutron detector; discriminates contamination type, used in some CT scanners
Which instrument is used to calibrate a linear accelerator's output?
Ionization chambers are the standard instrument for calibrating LINAC output and measuring beam characteristics.
Personal dosimeters fall into two categories:
(electronic dosimeters, pocket ionization chambers — give immediate readings) and
Immediate, accurate reading; but expensive, easily damaged, no permanent record
Film between metal filters (Al, Cu, Pb, or Sn)
Inexpensive and accurate; but can't be worn long-term, can fog from heat/humidity
Lithium fluoride (LiF) crystals emit light proportional to dose when heated
Reusable, won't fog, wearable up to 3 months; but no permanent record after readout
Aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) crystals, read via laser stimulation
More sensitive than film/TLD, can be reanalyzed, long-term stability
Monitors are worn at collar level, above the waist, near the thyroid — the area typically receiving the highest exposure. Declared Pregnant Workers wear a second badge at waist level.

General rules: never share badges, never intentionally expose them, report accidental exposure or contamination immediately, don't wear your badge during your own medical imaging/treatment, and never take it to another institution.

You accidentally leave your film badge on a counter near a treatment room overnight. What should you do?

options: Say nothing since it was an accident, and continue wearing it as normal
Report the possible accidental exposure immediately

content.text: Accidental badge exposures must be reported right away so the reading isn't misattributed to real occupational dose.

You've covered the three pillars of radiation protection, units of measurement, dose equivalent and effective dose calculations, occupational and public dose limits, pregnant worker policy, regulatory organizations, detection instruments, and personnel monitoring devices.
